reason: The blood sample and water loss suggest the first step in showing how reduced body water is detected.
expectation: The sample will become more concentrated as water is lost.

effect: The sample is more concentrated, so the next step is to connect it to the brain's water sensors.
reaction: The result matched the expected change.
reason: The sensors should detect the change in blood concentration and begin the water-saving response.
expectation: The sensors will respond to the concentrated blood and initiate a pituitary signal.

effect: The concentrated sample triggered ADH release into the blood; the responsive collecting ducts are the next likely target.
reaction: The sensor-to-hormone connection is clear, though ADH has not yet been defined.
reason: The collecting ducts have receptors for ADH, so they should respond to the hormone in blood.
expectation: ADH will make the collecting ducts conserve more water.

effect: ADH increased water recovery through collecting-duct channels, completing the first goal. The remaining goal calls for a body-wide control route and drinking water.
reaction: The contrast between the duct fluid and surrounding tissue makes the water movement clearer.
reason: The hormone-releasing nerve endings and pituitary blood vessels are positioned to connect the brain's signal to the bloodstream.
expectation: They will form a route for releasing the water-saving hormone into blood.

effect: The nerve endings and vessels formed the hormone-release route, which can now be connected to the body.
reaction: The route makes the link between the brain and blood more concrete.
reason: The body needs the newly constructed hormone route to complete its water-control system.
expectation: The body will gain a connected brain-to-kidney water-control route.

effect: The body now has a brain-to-kidney hormone route; the remaining goal also calls for a drink.
reaction: The connection follows the earlier ADH pathway as expected.
reason: Drinking water should complete the remaining water-replacement goal.
expectation: The body will take in water to help replace its losses.

effect: Drinking water entered the circulation, and the comparison showed ADH signalling decreasing as plasma concentration approached its usual range. Both goals are complete.
reaction: The feedback connection was a useful conclusion rather than just adding a drink to the model.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting ADH to the collecting ducts was most worthwhile: the planned illustration links receptors and additional water channels to water moving toward more concentrated surrounding tissue and back into blood.

leastWorthwhile.text: The separate construction and attachment of the brain-to-blood route repeated a connection already introduced when concentrated blood triggered ADH release, although it made the anatomy more concrete.

surprise.text: The final comparison added a feedback connection: as plasma concentration approached its usual range, fewer ADH signals left the pituitary.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though constructing the pituitary route separately after ADH had already appeared in blood felt somewhat artificial. ADH was also used without being expanded or defined.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the water-channel mechanism and the final feedback comparison made the system connections interesting, even if the separate route-building felt repetitive.
